text: ⦃⦅This section reviews the eight included studies of stream 3⦆, whose main contribution involves the participation of more than one party in a consent or access decision. ⦅Req 3 applies where a single party cannot lawfully authorise access on its own. In that case, a predefined number of designated parties must each provide an independently verifiable approval. This threshold condition must be represented within the consent object, and it must be possible for any party to check it at a later time.⦆ ⦅The background surveys and position papers [1]–[34] reviewed in Section 2.3 give the impression that multi-party joint authorisation of patient data access has not been realised in the literature. The full-text coding of the included studies does not support that impression.⦆ The full-text coding of the present corpus does not support that statement, and it is withdrawn. ⦅Across the 25 included studies, T3 (at least two distinct independent participants must approve) was graded Yes in 6 studies, Partial in 4 and No in 15,⦆ and the coding panel ratified six distinct mechanism classes of multi-party authorisation. ⦅It should be noted that the coding applied a strict word-sense discipline. Blockchain consensus, endorsement policies, multi-authority attribute-based encryption, secure multi-party computation parties, requester co-signatures and social key-recovery guardians were not counted as multi-party authorisation, because none of them adds an independent authoriser to the decision.⦆ The purpose of this section is therefore to state precisely which forms of multi-party authorisation exist and which form does not.⦄

⦃The first class is joint approval on a contingency path. Madine et al. [53] propose a fully decentralised multi-party consent scheme on Ethereum in which an access request on the incapacitated path requires the approvals of a regulatory agency and of at least the minimum of ceil(0.7g) and five guardians on the same request, and an emergency request requires the agency's approval together with a hospital admission confirmation. This is a genuine N-of-M condition over independent parties, combined with expiry enforced inside the decision predicate, since stale attestations stop counting, and with explicit revocation of claims and removal of guardians. ⦅However, on the normal path a single patient key authorises access. Joint approval is therefore a fallback that applies only when the principal is absent, and it is not a condition of every decision.⦆ In addition, the guardians hold no key shares: the decryption key is split between the patient and the regulatory agency, which can decrypt with its own shares, so the joint guarantee holds at the smart-contract layer only. The paper contains no formal analysis, no dataset and no allow or deny correctness matrix. A related design is threshold key custody. Abbasi et al. ⦅[35] present Nexa, a public-blockchain record system in which a Shamir (5, 3) threshold protects each record key. A clinical access combines the requester's own share with two automated oracle shares released on the basis of the current on-chain role. There is therefore a single authorisation locus and no human co-approval, and the patient's share is not required. The institutional multi-signature for bulk access is proposed but outside the prototype.⦆ The prototype is public and measured, but no authorisation decision is verified. The threshold over patient-designated relatives of Maruthi and Singh [54], reviewed in Section 2.4.6, belongs to the same custody class.⦄

⦃The second class places the threshold on the institution side. Wu et al. [75] present Soteria, a clinical-trial data platform on Hyperledger Fabric with trusted-execution chaincode in which a (t, n) threshold signature runs over named investigators. ⦅The threshold does not apply to all operations in the same way. The admission of a trial record to the ledger requires a majority of investigators and the revocation of a consent requires half of them, whereas the consent grant itself is submitted unilaterally by the patient.⦆ ⦅In addition, each investigator's vote consists of recomputing and confirming the hash of the message,⦆ so the threshold is a threshold of integrity verifiers rather than of authorisers, and the voters act for the institution rather than for the patient. The third class is institutional custodian approval conjoined with a policy engine. ⦅Punia et al. [61] implement MedXBlock, a permissioned Ethereum access-control system. In this system, an M-of-N multi-signature contract over registered doctors and administrators, for example two of three, governs high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests. An implemented hybrid attribute- and role-based policy engine evaluates a conjunctive grant predicate with deny-by-default over a stateful policy store.⦆ ⦅This is the only study among the 25 included studies in which⦆ multi-party approval and an enforced policy predicate co-occur. ⦅Even so, the threshold applies only to high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests, since ordinary access is token-only, and it can be bypassed by a single emergency officer. In addition, it is implemented outside the grant predicate as a separate layer.⦆⦅ The patient enters the predicate as a boolean consent attribute rather than as an authoriser, and no purpose term exists. The assurance is a threat table and an asserted safety property, and the 100 measured transactions include no executed authorisation test.⦆⦄

⦃The fourth class appoints witnesses. ⦅Tan et al. [69] propose a personal health record sharing scheme with multi-party pre-authorisation verification, in which the patient fixes n verifiers and a threshold t. Each verifier evaluates the patient-issued grant, its expiry and the revocation list before releasing its share of the decryption key. Without t shares, no key and no plaintext exist.⦆ This is the first threshold in the corpus whose authorisers are appointed by the patient for the patient's own access decision, and expiry is checked at the point of approval. ⦅The joint approval is nevertheless a pre-delegated contingency for the case in which the patient is unable to act. The verifiers evaluate identity, grant, time and revocation but not purpose or data scope, since attribute-based policy is explicitly future work. Only the secure multi-party computation layer is implemented, while the identity, wallet and ledger layers are not. The security argument is a STRIDE and LINDDUN enumeration with no proof over the authorisation protocol.⦆ The fifth class, reviewed in Section 2.4.6, is the consumer-side delegated threshold of Zhao and Su [50], in which l of d already-authorised clinicians jointly authorise an out-of-policy requester; the delegates are consumer-side rather than patient-side parties, and the scheme has no time, lifecycle or purpose term.⦄

⦃The sixth class is register-verified guardian co-consent at consent registration, and it is the only class found in deployed systems. Ekholm et al. ⦅[43] report the implementation of electronic informed consent in rare disease genomics on a commercial platform used by three genomic medicine centres in Sweden. The consent of a minor is valid only when all legal guardians, one or two, have signed. Guardianship is verified in real time against the national Population Register, and 61 paediatric trio consents were obtained under this rule.⦆ This is a deployed n-of-n guardian condition with authority verified separately from the national electronic identity used for authentication, and it is the cleanest separation of identity and authority in the corpus. ⦅However, the condition applies at the registration of consent and not at the access decision. The only decision-time touchpoint is an interface that answers whether a valid consent exists, without purpose, scope or time parameters. The platform is centralised, and the paper provides no formal or authorisation-correctness evidence.⦆ ⦅Hagström et al. [47] examine the national patient portals of Sweden and Finland in a retrospective comparative case study. In both portals, guardian proxy access to a minor's record is gated jointly by a healthcare professional's assessment of the minor's capacity and by the minor's own consent, and guardianship is verified against a population register. Age windows are also enforced, and their enforcement is demonstrated by the absence of use within blocked windows and by the consent of 95.8 per cent of capable minors to disclosure.⦆ This is a second deployed instance of collective, consent-gated proxy governance, but it is documentation-time governance in centralised national systems with no formal assurance. Finally, Al Amin et al. [38] represent informed consent as a patient-driven policy IC = (U, O, OP, CON), an evaluable object whose contextual conditions include time, date, day, location, network address and access frequency, and whose enforcement conjoins the patient's consent with organisational and regulatory policies. ⦅The only multi-party element is a two-of-two multi-signature wallet in the experimental harness, in which every member must sign to store a consent. The members are not named, the mechanism gates registration rather than access, and it is absent from the model. No purpose term exists, and the Goerli deployment reports no measured result or allow or deny case.⦆ The panel recorded it as a candidate class only.⦄

⦅The position of the literature with respect to Req 3 can therefore be stated precisely. What exists is multi-party authorisation in six forms. The first two are joint approval on a contingency path when the principal is absent [53, 69], and guardian or bilateral co-consent at the time of consent registration [43, 47, 38]. The next two are institution-side thresholds over record admission and consent revocation [75], and custodial M-of-N approval around, but not inside, a policy predicate [61]. The last two are a patient-appointed witness threshold welded to key release [69], and threshold key custody or delegation among custodians, relatives or clinicians [35, 54, 50]. In this context, the sentence that multi-party authorisation does not exist in the literature is no longer defensible and is not made in this review. ⦅What does not exist in any of the 25 included studies⦆ is a threshold predicate over the guardian set G with threshold N that is constitutive of the access decision. Such a predicate would be evaluated on every access request in a decentralised exchange. It would be a conjunct of the same predicate that evaluates the policy conditions of purpose and data scope, the temporal validity and the jurisdiction of the consent object C. It would also be supported by allow and deny correctness evidence and by formal assurance of the conjunction. The coding supports each element of this statement. Only Punia et al. [61] combine T3 = Yes with an enforced policy predicate, and there the threshold is outside the predicate, the patient is an attribute and purpose is absent. ⦅Every T3-positive study in this stream is graded No or Partial on Req 6, except the observational study of Hagström et al. [47], whose Req 6 tick rests on empirical evidence alone. The two T3-positive studies elsewhere that carry a proof [50, 54] prove the threshold gate or confidentiality in isolation. Therefore, the broadest multi-party systems carry the weakest assurance.⦆ In addition, the deployed guardian mechanisms [43, 47] establish guardian authority through a state register, which is the attestation pattern against which the guardian credentials of the proposed framework must be compared. ⦅Table 5 presents a summary of the eight included studies in this stream⦆ and their commitment to the key requirements.⦆

The consent grant is unilateral and the threshold governs record admission and revocation rather than the patient's access decision; each vote is a hash-integrity check by institution-side investigators; time is a stored attribute not shown to gate the decision; no policy engine; no theorem, proof or adversary model; performance only with borrowed latency figures and no correctness or attack evaluation.

text: ⦃Healthcare access-control research has developed a broad range of mechanisms for restricting access according to roles, attributes, risk conditions and usage constraints. Attribute-based encryption and decentralised key management protect healthcare data through cryptographic access policies [32], risk-aware usage-control models incorporate dynamic conditions beyond role-based permissions [11], and recent surveys of blockchain-based and IoT healthcare access control emphasise fine-grained, dynamic and privacy-preserving enforcement [28, 25]. ⦅This section reviews the four included studies of stream 4⦆ against Req 4. ⦅The question asked of each study is not whether a policy exists. It is whether purpose, data scope, requester role and contextual constraints influence the decision at the time of access. It is also whether the evaluated policy is bound to the consent object rather than to the requester alone.⦆ It should be noted that, under the coding rules of Section 2.3, a policy that is described in prose or stored on a ledger without being consulted by the decision does not satisfy Req 4.⦄

⦃Tith et al. [71] proposed one of the earliest purpose-based consent models for electronic health records on a Hyperledger Fabric consortium. Consent is represented as an evaluable four-tuple of role, doctor identifiers, action and intended purpose, in which the intended purpose is expressed through a purpose tree with allowed and prohibited purposes, and the tuple is matched by chaincode at request time with per-datum scope. The model therefore satisfies Req 1 and Req 4. ⦅However, the consent tuple carries no temporal element. Withdrawal is implemented in chaincode, but its effect on subsequent access is not tested. Identity rests on the Fabric membership service without decentralised identifiers or authority credentials. The prototype on four nodes reports functional targets without quantitative results, attack cases or a formal argument.⦆ ⦅Jaiman and Urovi [49] developed a consent model for blockchain-based health data sharing platforms. In this model, the purpose of a request is matched inside the smart contract against the patient's consent. The matching uses the Data Use Ontology and the Automatable Discovery and Access Matrix ontology, and denial is tested across several requester profiles.⦆ This is one of the few studies in the corpus in which purpose is evaluated in the decision and the denial path is exercised. Security assurance is explicitly placed outside the scope of the paper, the consent is granted by a single patient, and temporal validity and lifecycle transitions are not enforced in the decision.⦄

⦃Albalwy et al. [37] presented ConsentChain, a dynamic consent architecture for clinical genomic data sharing on a permissioned Ethereum network. Consent is a machine-readable object of data type, role and purpose, combined into an access-policy tree that is hashed and evaluated by a checkConsent function, so that purpose, role and data type are jointly required. ⦅The evaluation is a rigid exact-match of hashes rather than a policy engine, and the requester role is self-submitted and not verified against a credential. The consent tuple has no validity interval, and time is applied only at the data-delivery layer through short-lived download links. Revocation is a binary active or cancelled status, and the security analysis is qualitative.⦆ The proof of concept is deployed in a production environment with measured throughput and open source code, but no adversarial or systematic allow-and-deny tests are reported. Román-Martínez et al. [63] proposed a blockchain-based service-oriented architecture for consent management, access control and auditing in which FHIR Consent purpose-of-use limits are evaluated per resource by an XACML policy decision point operating over Hyperledger Fabric. This is the most standards-native purpose enforcement in the corpus, and the architecture includes supervisory auditing. Nevertheless, no withdrawal or expiry path exists anywhere in the architecture, and the authors state that their experiments validate the blockchain component only, so the authorisation decision itself is not verified.⦄

⦅⦅Across the 25 included studies, T4 is coded Yes in 11, Partial in 10 and No in 4.⦆ A policy or attribute condition therefore influences the access decision in a substantial share of the reviewed systems, and the requirement cannot be described as unaddressed. However, the nature of the policy is narrower than Req 4 demands. In most of the T4-positive studies the evaluated policy is bound to the requester, that is, to a role, a department, an institution or an attribute set. This is the case in Punia et al. [61], in Li et al. [51], in the attribute-based access control of Ghosh et al. [46] and in the attribute-based encryption schemes of stream 6. ⦅Purpose-of-use enters the evaluated decision in only six of the 25 included studies [37, 44, 49, 57, 63, 71], and in one supporting reference [45].⦆ Purpose and data scope are jointly present in the decision by design in fewer still, in Albalwy et al. [37], Eneh et al. [44], ⦅Tith et al. [71] and the supporting reference [45].⦆ ⦅Jurisdiction appears as a rule field only in Eneh et al. [44]; other contextual conditions are limited to the duty-hours term of Punia et al. [61] and the location and network-address conditions specified but not enforced by Al Amin et al. [38].⦆ The gap verdicts recorded by the coding panel repeatedly note the absence of a purpose or data-category policy from the decision. Madine et al. [53] contain no purpose or policy term in the body of the paper, Tan et al. [69] defer attribute-based scope to future work, Punia et al. [61] evaluate role, department, record type and duty hours but no purpose, and Hema et al. [64] scope keys by role and workflow but carry no purpose-of-use term in the consent token. It should also be noted that every purpose-bearing study is coded T3 No. The single study which conjoins an implemented policy engine with a threshold approval, Punia et al. [61], consumes patient consent as a boolean attribute rather than as a consent object with its own scope. ⦅Therefore, the residual deficit for Req 4 is not the absence of a policy engine. The deficit is that purpose-of-use and data-scope constraints are not carried by the consent object C itself⦆ and evaluated together with the identity, authority and multi-party conditions, with evidence that requests outside the authorised scope are refused. ⦅Table 6 presents a summary of the four included studies of stream 4⦆ and their commitment to the key requirements.⦆

⦃⦅Supporting reference. One further report of stream 4 was coded and retained outside the corpus.⦆ The quantum-safe attribute-based access control scheme of Ghosh et al. ⦅[46] corroborates the finding that an attribute policy can operate inside the access decision and be enforced cryptographically, with attribute revocation checked at every access. It also confirms the residual deficit. The policy carries no purpose-of-use or data-scope term, one fully trusted authority issues and verifies both identity and authority, and the security analysis is argued without a theorem or tool.⦆⦄

text: ⦃Req 5 requires that the validity interval of a consent and its lifecycle state are technically enforced inside the authorisation decision. Two distinctions from the codebook of Section 2.3 govern the reading of this stream. First, a timestamp that is written to a log or stored in a consent record is not temporal authorisation; the decision itself must read the clock. Second, a mention of revocation, or an operation that changes a status field, is not an implemented lifecycle unless the state is consulted by the decision and the transitions are constrained. ⦅This section reviews the four included studies of stream 5⦆, namely Eneh et al. [44], Li et al. [51], Panagoulias et al. [57] and Hema et al. [64], and draws on the lifecycle evidence ⦅recorded for the included studies of the other streams⦆.⦄

⦃Eneh et al. [44] presented EdgeConsent, an on-chain attribute-based access control engine for data consent management, demonstrated on a healthcare scenario. Consent rules carry not-before and not-after bounds together with roles, organisations, jurisdictions, data categories, sensitivity levels, purposes and actions, and the checkAccess function evaluates the requester attributes, the resource, the purpose and the current timestamp against these bounds with deny-by-default and deny-overrides semantics. Expiry therefore takes effect at decision time, and the demonstration shows that a request is denied again once its rule is revoked. This is the first study in the corpus in which temporal validity is enforced inside the decision predicate. ⦅The lifecycle is nevertheless limited to an active flag and the temporal bounds, without pending, suspended or renewed states. Identity is a wallet address with an attribute registry whose issuance governance is unspecified, and a single patient authors the rules. There is no threat model. The evaluation is a two-page demonstration on a local network with gas measurements and an integration test suite.⦆ ⦅

Hema et al. [64] take a different approach in a patient-centric cryptographic protection scheme for cloud EHRs.⦆⦅ In this scheme the patient's signed consent token, the requester role and the expiry time are inputs to the key derivation function. Once the expiry has passed, the decryption key cannot be reconstructed, and revocation likewise causes derivation to fail without re-encryption.⦆ ⦅Therefore, the expiry is enforced by the key derivation itself rather than by an explicit comparison in a decision function, and authority is separated from identity through role-scoped keys.⦆⦅⦆ ⦅However, there is no lifecycle state machine, and the consent is issued by a single patient key. Identity relies on a commercial authentication service without credentials. The security argument is an adversary model with a probabilistic statement rather than a proof, and only operation latency is measured.⦆ ⦅Panagoulias et al. [57] proposed a blockchain-enabled governance overlay for clinical artificial intelligence pipelines. In this overlay, a formal policy object carries identifiers, roles, purposes, a validity window and a revoked flag with a version number. Access is allowed only if the policy is valid at time t and the role and purpose conditions hold.⦆ Revocation is enforced mid-stream at decision time and is verified through a consent-drift metric over 43,500 simulated attempts across nine scenarios, with denials recorded as ledger events. ⦅The temporal conjunct is implemented, but interval-bound denials are not separately exercised, and the lifecycle is a binary active or revoked state. The ledger is a single-node hash chain without consensus, and identity is inherited from an existing clinical identity provider. The authors explicitly declare that no formal verification was performed.⦆⦄

⦃⦅The fourth included study illustrates⦆ a pattern that the coding panel describes as displacement, in which time is enforced on an artefact issued to the requester rather than on the consent itself. Li et al. ⦅[51] presented a hybrid role-based and smart-contract scheme with attribute-based authorisation for IoMT records. The expiry of a signed credential is compared with the current time at every sharing interaction, and a grant ledger records authorisations. The credential window is therefore enforced. However, the consent or authorisation object itself carries no enforced validity window, and there is no consent state machine.⦆ The same displacement is observed in the short-lived tokens of Tseng et al. [73] in stream 2, whose expiry is checked by the token validator while revocation of the access-control list does not invalidate tokens already issued. In both cases the enforced time belongs to a credential or a token, and the consent object is left without a validity interval of its own.⦄

⦅⦅Across the 25 included studies, T5 is coded Yes in 8 and T6 in 7. Req 5, which requires enforcement in the decision, is Yes in 8.⦆⦆⦃ The distinction between recorded and enforced time explains most of the Partial codes. Albalwy et al. [37], for example, store a struct timestamp in the consent record and apply time only to the download link, so that the consent tuple itself has no validity interval. A parallel distinction separates named state machines from ad hoc revocation flags. Named states with constrained transitions appear in Phuyal et al. [58] (active and revoked with an audited emergency override), Wu et al. [75] (approved, pending, completed and revoked with investigator-verified transitions) and Punia et al. [61], although in the last case the states belong to policies and tokens rather than to the consent. By contrast, Abbasi et al. [35] enforce a role status without consent states, and even Madine et al. [53], with four transitions that affect the decision, define no named state set. Where revocation is enforced at scheme level, as in the immediate ciphertext update of Mei et al. [55], its cost is measured but its effect on a revoked requester is not exercised; ⦅among the included studies a post-revocation denial⦆ is actually demonstrated only by Phuyal et al. [58], Panagoulias et al. [57] and Eneh et al. [44]. In this context, the residual deficit for Req 5 is not the absence of decision-time temporal enforcement, which Eneh et al. [44], Hema et al. [64] and Panagoulias et al. [57] each achieve in isolation. ⦅The deficit is that temporal and lifecycle enforcement at the level of the consent object has not been verified in a deployed multi-institution exchange.⦆⦅ In addition, the three stream-5 systems which enforce time inside the decision are all single-party. ⦅Of the eight included studies coded Yes on Req 5⦆, including the multi-party designs of Madine et al. [53] and Punia et al. [61], only the encryption scheme of Mei et al. [55] carries a formal proof. That proof concerns the static encryption predicate rather than the consent decision.⦆ ⦅Table 7 presents a summary of the included stream-5 studies⦆ and their commitment to the key requirements.⦄

⦃⦅Supporting reference. One further report of stream 5 was coded and retained outside the corpus.⦆ ⦅The revocable attribute-based encryption scheme of Xu et al. [77], organised in key epochs for hospital-to-hospital sharing, corroborates the displacement pattern. Revocation is realised by key rollover, so that a revoked user retains access until the epoch ends. The word consent does not appear, and keyword matching is a discovery mechanism rather than an approval.⦆ ⦅The distinction between recorded and enforced time is likewise ⦅corroborated by the supporting references of the other streams⦆. In several of them a timestamp is stored, logged or used only as a replay window without being read by the decision [46], [60], [62], [78]. In others, automatic expiry is claimed without specifying where the clock is read [68], [70]. ⦅Among the supporting references, a post-revocation denial⦆ is reported only in results captioned as illustrative [45] or in a single narrated scenario [68]. Named consent states gating the decision appear ⦅in one further supporting reference [66]⦆.⦆⦄

title: Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation

text: ⦃Req 6 has two components. ⦅The first is that the security properties of the authorisation mechanism are formally defined and demonstrated. This may be done through a security proof, a model, a verification tool or an explicit adversary model with a theorem. Under the codebook, the statement that a system is secure is not evidence, and a threat discussion alone is coded Partial.⦆ The second is that the mechanism is validated empirically, through a prototype, a dataset, allow-and-deny test cases, attack cases or audit evidence; architecture diagrams alone are not empirical validation. In the workbook these two components are coded separately as Req6 and Req7, and they are combined into the report's Req 6 in the tables of this chapter. ⦅Stream 6 gathers the four included studies⦆ in which formal argument is a principal contribution, namely Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54], Mei et al. [55] and Wu and Zhang [76], all of them cryptographic constructions published in security and network journals.⦄

⦃Wu and Zhang [76] presented HealthDID, an authorisable multi-party privacy-preserving EMR sharing system based on decentralised identifiers. The authorisation proof is a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof that binds the data subject's commitment to the public key of a specific queryer, so that a verifier can check that this subject authorised this requester without learning the subject's identity; ⦅authorisation is therefore separated from the DID challenge-response authentication.⦆ The paper states three game-based security definitions and proves three theorems by reduction, namely anonymity from the hiding property of Pedersen commitments, unforgeability of the authorisation proof from the discrete logarithm assumption through the forking lemma, and search privacy from the decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption. ⦅This is the first complete formal assurance in the corpus. However, what is proven concerns the identity and authority fragment only.⦆ ⦅There is no theorem of the form that access is granted only under stated conditions. The proofs cannot cover policy, temporal or lifecycle conjuncts because the system has none. Access is all-or-nothing per authorising owner, the only time values are index and document fields that no algorithm reads, and there is no revocation, withdrawal or state.⦆ The term multi-party denotes several stakeholders whose privacy requirements are satisfied simultaneously, not several parties authorising one decision. ⦅The evaluation is a reproducible performance study with a public repository, but it includes no allow-and-deny tests, executed attacks or dataset.⦆ ⦅Zhao and Su [50] proposed a threshold traceable delegation authorisation scheme in which the data owner delegates to l of d already-authorised users. Each of these users must run an authorisation algorithm bound to a private key before an out-of-policy requester can restore the data. Unforgeability below the threshold rests on the bilinear Diffie-Hellman assumption, and confidentiality is proven under an IND-CPA game with reduction.⦆ The proof covers the threshold gate in isolation, the delegates are consumer-side clinicians rather than patient-side stakeholders, there is no time, expiry, revocation or state, and the Java benchmark measures performance only. ⦅Maruthi and Singh [54] addressed the unconscious patient with a threshold proxy re-encryption scheme. In this scheme t of n patient-designated relatives contribute to re-encryption without the key ever being reassembled at a single point. The hospital and the relatives are authenticated on chain through non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs, and IND-CCA security is proven. A Solidity implementation is reported.⦆ The collective mechanism is genuine and decision-time, but policy and temporal conditions are both absent, so the proof again covers a narrow predicate. Mei et al. ⦅[55] proposed a dual-revocation ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption scheme for IoMT in which a direct mode terminates access immediately through a ciphertext update. The authors motivate this construction by patient consent withdrawal. The scheme offers user-level and attribute-level granularity and an IND-CPA reduction under the q-BDHE assumption. It has no audit element and no multi-party approval, and the proof concerns the static encryption predicate.⦆⦄

⦅Two observations follow at corpus level. The first concerns formal assurance in the sense of the workbook's Req6. ⦅It is coded Yes in only 4 of the 25 included studies, all of them in this stream. Two supporting references of this stream, both encryption schemes, also carry a proof.⦆ In every case the proven property attaches to a narrow predicate. It is an identity-and-authority fragment in HealthDID [76], a threshold gate in Zhao and Su [50] and Maruthi and Singh [54], and a static attribute policy in the encryption scheme of Mei et al. [55]. By contrast, the studies with the broadest decision predicates carry the weakest assurance. Punia et al. [61], with six of seven dimensions positive, offer a threat table and an asserted safety property. Madine et al. [53], the strongest multi-party system, contain no adversary model, property statement or proof. Panagoulias et al. [57], whose decision is the best verified in the corpus, state that no formal method was applied. The coding panel records this as an inverse relation between predicate breadth and assurance strength, and the quadrant in which a broad conjunctive predicate is also formally assured is empty. Structured threat models in the STRIDE or LINDDUN style, as in Tan et al. [69], Phuyal et al. [59] and Panagoulias et al. [57], are useful, but they were coded Partial because they enumerate threats without demonstrating properties.⦆

⦅The second observation concerns empirical validation in the sense of the workbook's Req7. ⦅It is coded Yes in only 5 of the 25 included studies, Partial in 19 and No in 1.⦆ In the large majority of the Partial cases, evaluation means throughput, latency, gas cost, block time or encryption timing. Abbasi et al. [35] measure hundreds to a thousand transactions per operation on a public test network with a published repository and a Synthea-generated dataset, but execute no allow-or-deny test. Punia et al. [61] instrument 100 transactions and describe, but do not run, the single denial scenario. The four cryptographic studies of this stream report benchmarks of their primitives without exercising a single denial. The coding panel describes this pattern as built and measured but never validated as an authorisation decision, and it is the dominant form of evidence in the corpus. Negative validation of the decision, that is, evidence that requests without sufficient authority, outside the authorised scope or after revocation are refused, is found in a small minority. Panagoulias et al. [57] report a blocked rate of 1.000 for unauthorised attempts and zero post-revocation drift across 43,500 attempts, in a single-node simulation. Phuyal et al. [58] test allow and deny paths over 100 runs per workflow and show that revocation yields a refused access within about 1.5 seconds, in a simulated hospital without adversarial tests. Jaiman and Urovi [49] test denial across requester profiles, Albalwy et al. [37] deploy a proof of concept with open code but without adversarial tests, and Hagström et al. [47] show that age windows in a national portal are enforced in practice. No study executes an adversarial campaign against the authorisation decision itself. Where adversarial testing exists, it targets ledger integrity, as in Panagoulias et al. [57], or the software surface through penetration testing, as in Tremper et al. [72]. Therefore, the residual deficit for Req 6 is the combination, within one system, of a formal argument over the conjoined identity, authority, multi-party, policy and temporal conditions and an audited set of allow and deny cases that includes the negative cases. ⦅Table 8 presents a summary of the included stream-6 studies⦆ and their commitment to the key requirements.⦆

⦅Supporting references. Five further reports of stream 6 were coded and retained outside the corpus. Two of them are coded Yes on formal assurance. These are the revocable attribute-based searchable encryption scheme of Gao et al. [48] and the bilateral proxy re-encryption scheme of Luo et al. [52]. They corroborate the first observation, since each proof concerns a static encryption predicate. The threshold among authorisation nodes in [48] is key-management resilience rather than approval, and the bilateral matching in [52] is policy symmetry rather than co-approval. The private set intersection protocol of Cao et al. [40], the lightweight multi-authority CP-ABE scheme of Qiao et al. [62] and the policy-hiding encryption scheme of Zhang et al. [56] were coded Partial on formal assurance because their proofs do not reach the authorisation decision, and all five corroborate the second observation, since their evaluations are timing benchmarks or simulations without allow-and-deny or attack tests.⦆

text: ⦅The reviewed literature demonstrates that existing approaches provide strong solutions for individual dimensions of trustworthy consent authorisation. Evaluable consent objects that are consulted at the time of a request have existed since 2020 in the purpose-based models of Tith et al. [71] and Jaiman and Urovi [49]. They are now realised with richer attributes in Eneh et al. [44], Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58]. The separation of identity from authority is achieved through licensing-body credentials in Phuyal et al. [58], through a national population register in Ekholm et al. [43], through a requester-bound zero-knowledge authorisation proof in HealthDID [76] and through role-scoped key derivation in Hema et al. [64]. Multi-party mechanisms exist in six distinct classes. These include the guardian and agency approvals of Madine et al. [53], the patient-appointed verifiers of Tan et al. [69], the delegated threshold of Zhao and Su [50], the institutional multi-signature of Punia et al. [61], the kin threshold of Maruthi and Singh [54] and the deployed guardian co-consent of Ekholm et al. [43]. Policy engines operate inside the decision in Punia et al. [61] and Román-Martínez et al. [63]. Temporal validity is enforced inside the decision by Eneh et al. [44], Hema et al. [64] and Madine et al. [53]. Formal proofs are given for the identity fragment of HealthDID [76] and for several threshold and encryption schemes. Verified allow-and-deny behaviour is reported by Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58].⦆

⦅However, these contributions address different layers of the same problem, and the strength of each study on one requirement coincides with an absence on another. The systems that enforce purpose and time inside the decision are authored by a single patient and provide no formal argument. The systems that provide multi-party approval carry no purpose or data-scope condition and no formal argument. The schemes that prove security properties do so for predicates that contain no policy, no temporal validity and no lifecycle. A blockchain record does not establish participant authority, a valid identifier does not establish permission, an approval threshold does not guarantee that the request lies within the authorised scope, and a proof of unforgeability does not state the conditions under which access is granted. Consequently, no reviewed study establishes that a healthcare data-access decision is trustworthy in the conjunctive sense required by Section 2.2. In that sense, the identity, authority, multi-party, policy and temporal conditions must hold together, and this conjunction must be both formally argued and empirically tested.⦆

[37] and Li et al. [51]. The core studies are those whose coding narrows, weakens or contradicts one of the deficits of the gap statement. Studies that carry a multi-party signal (T3 Yes or Partial) are also core studies.⦆ ⦅The 19 supporting references are cited in the supporting-reference paragraphs of Sections 2.4.1 to 2.4.6 and are outside the corpus, so that the comparison rests on the studies closest to the research problem.⦆ The ticks are taken from the coding of Section 2.3, with Req 6 combining the coding scheme's formal-assurance and empirical-validation codes as explained in Section 2.4.6.⦄

text: ⦅The matrix supports four observations. First, counting only full satisfaction, ⦅Req 1 is met by 12 of the 25 included studies⦆, Req 2 by 7, Req 3 by 6, Req 4 by 10, Req 5 by 8 and Req 6 by 9. No requirement is unaddressed. However, ⦅none is met by a majority of the included studies⦆, and Req 1, at 12 of 25, comes closest. Second, no study satisfies all six requirements together. The largest number of requirements fully satisfied by a single study is four. This number is reached by Madine et al. [53] on Req 1, Req 2, Req 3 and Req 5 and by Panagoulias et al. [57] on Req 1, Req 4, Req 5 and Req 6. Six studies, namely Abbasi et al. [35], Al Amin et al. [38], Hagström et al. [47], Madine et al. [53], Punia et al. [61] and Wu et al. [75], carry no cross in any column, but each of them relies on Partial codes for at least two requirements. Five studies, namely Abbasi et al. [35], Phuyal et al. [59], Soohoo et al. [67], Tremper et al. [72] and Wu et al. [75], fully satisfy no requirement at all. Third, the pair of requirements that co-occurs most often is Req 1 with Req 4, which is found in seven studies (Albalwy et al. [37], Eneh et al. [44], Jaiman and Urovi [49], Panagoulias et al. [57], Román-Martínez et al. [63], Hema et al. [64] and Tith et al. [71]). The next most frequent pair is Req 4 with Req 5, which is found in six studies (Eneh et al. [44], Li et al. [51], Mei et al. [55], Panagoulias et al. [57], Punia et al. [61] and Hema et al. [64]). These two pairs reflect the maturity of single-party consent objects with purpose and time conditions. In contrast, Req 2 and Req 4 never co-occur in full. Req 3 co-occurs with Req 4 only in Punia et al. [61]. Req 3 co-occurs with Req 6 only in the two cryptographic threshold schemes of Zhao and Su [50] and Maruthi and Singh [54], neither of which has policy or temporal enforcement. Two triples are the most frequent, and each is found in three studies. The first is Req 1 with Req 4 and Req 5, in Eneh et al. [44], Panagoulias et al. [57] and Hema et al. [64], all of them single-party systems. The second is Req 1 with Req 4 and Req 6, in Albalwy et al. [37], Jaiman and Urovi [49] and Panagoulias et al. [57], all of them single-party systems whose Req 6 tick rests on empirical validation rather than a formal proof. The triples that include Req 3 are fewer. Req 1, Req 2 and Req 3 co-occur in Madine et al. [53] and in Tan et al. [69], neither of which enforces purpose or data scope or provides a formal argument; the quadruple of Madine et al. [53] also yields Req 1 or Req 2 with Req 3 and Req 5. Req 3, Req 4 and Req 5 co-occur in Punia et al. [61], where the threshold lies outside the policy predicate and no purpose term exists. Fourth, ⦅the two quadruples among the included studies⦆ share only Req 1 and Req 5 and are otherwise complementary in the way that the gap predicts. Madine et al. [53] combine multi-party approval with identity, consent representation and time, but not with policy or assurance. Panagoulias et al. [57] combine consent representation, policy, time and validation, but not with multi-party approval or identity depth.⦆

⦅The comparison therefore indicates that the principal contribution of the proposed framework is not the replacement of existing technologies, each of which the literature has developed to a high standard in isolation. The contribution lies in establishing an explicit and verifiable relationship among them. In the proposed framework the consent object C carries the identity, authority, multi-party threshold, purpose and data-scope, temporal and lifecycle conditions together. The authorisation decision is the conjunction of their independent verification, and this conjunction is both formally argued and validated through positive and negative test cases. No reviewed study occupies this integrated position, which is represented by the final row of Table 9. The next section states the resulting research gap requirement by requirement.⦆

⦅This section synthesises the review of Section 2.4 against the six requirements defined in Section 2.2. The counts stated in this section refer to the 25 included studies. Across the corpus, the requirement that is most often satisfied is the representation of consent as an evaluable authorisation object (Req 1), which 12 studies satisfy fully and 13 satisfy in part. Policy- and context-aware enforcement (Req 4) is satisfied fully by 10 studies, in part by 11 and not at all by 4. Temporal validity and lifecycle control (Req 5) is satisfied fully by 8 studies, in part by 13 and not at all by 4. Decentralised verification of identity and authority (Req 2) is satisfied fully by 7 studies and in part by 18, and no included study is without an identity mechanism. Multi-party authorisation through a verifiable threshold (Req 3) is the least satisfied requirement: 6 studies satisfy it fully, 4 satisfy it in part and 15 do not address it. With respect to Req 6, formal security assurance of the authorisation decision is provided by 4 studies and argued informally by 9, while 12 studies offer no security analysis beyond assertion; empirical validation is complete in 5 studies, partial in 19 and absent in 1. It should be noted that these proportions are consistent with the signal prevalence in the wider full-text pool of 1,800 records described in Section 2.3.6, as recorded by the signal detectors of the screening workbook, in which only 8% of the records carry a multi-party signal, 2% a temporal-validity signal and 1% a formal-verification signal, compared with 74% for audit or evidence and 69% for a prototype or experiment. The scarcity observed among the included studies is therefore a property of the field and not an artefact of the selection.⦆

⦅It should be noted that the most important correction which the review makes to the framing of this research concerns multi-party authorisation.⦆⦃ ⦅Read on their own, the background surveys [1]–[34] suggest that multi-party authorisation of patient consent does not exist in the literature. The full-text coding does not support that suggestion.⦆ That statement is withdrawn. The coding panel identified six distinct mechanism classes in which more than one party participates in an authorisation-related decision. Madine et al. [53] require regulator and guardian approvals on a single access request, but only on the incapacitated and emergency paths; on the normal path a single patient key authorises, so that joint approval is a contingency rather than a standing condition. Wu et al. [75] apply a (t, n) threshold of investigators, but the threshold governs the admission of a trial record to the ledger and the revocation of a consent rather than the grant, and the vote itself reduces to a hash-integrity check. Zhao and Su [50] place the threshold among consumer-side delegates who are already within the access policy, and Tan et al. [69] place it among patient-appointed witnesses who act for a patient who is unable to act. Punia et al. [61] conjoin an institutional M-of-N signature with an attribute policy, but the signature is reserved for high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests, lies outside the decision predicate and can be bypassed by a single emergency officer. ⦅Ekholm et al. [43] report a deployed platform in which all legal guardians must co-sign at consent registration, and Hagström et al. [47] report national patient portals in which guardian proxy access is gated by register-verified guardianship, a professional's capacity assessment and the minor's own consent.⦆ In addition, Maruthi and Singh [54] distribute a threshold key among patient-designated relatives, and Abbasi et al. [35] among automated oracles, so that the threshold protects key custody rather than expressing an authorisation judgement. ⦅Therefore, multi-party approval exists in the reviewed literature in six forms. The first three are joint approval on a contingency path with key-share reconstruction, an institution-side admission gate and a consumer-side delegated threshold. The other three are a patient-appointed witness threshold, a custodial M-of-N around a policy engine and a guardian co-consent at consent registration.⦆ ⦅No reviewed study treats it as a constitutive predicate that every access decision must satisfy together with the identity, policy and temporal conditions. In addition, no study defines the approving set through the patient and evaluates it on every request.⦆⦄

⦃A similar qualification applies to Req 4 and Req 5. Purpose of use is evaluated inside the decision in several studies. Tith et al. [71] and Albalwy et al. [37] match a purpose tree or a purpose tuple, Jaiman and Urovi [49] match ontology terms, Román-Martínez et al. [63] evaluate the FHIR purpose-of-use through an XACML decision point, Eneh et al. [44] evaluate purpose, data category and jurisdiction in an on-chain rule set, and Panagoulias et al. [57] verify a purpose conjunct at scale. However, every one of these studies is single-party, and the one study that conjoins a policy engine with a multi-party signature, Punia et al. [61], carries no purpose term and consumes consent as a Boolean attribute. In the cryptographic schemes the policy is bound to the ciphertext or to the requester's attributes rather than to the consent [78, 46, 56], and in the deployed research infrastructures the purpose is displayed or logged rather than evaluated [72, 74, 73]. Purpose and data-scope policy that is bound to the consent object and conjoined with multi-party approval is therefore largely absent. Temporal enforcement inside the decision is rare. Eneh et al. [44] evaluate the validity bounds of a rule at request time, the key-derivation scheme in [64] binds the expiry into the key so that decryption after expiry is unreachable, Madine et al. [53] discount stale attestations, and Punia et al. [61] check token expiry on access. ⦅In most other studies the time element takes one of four forms. It is a stored timestamp [37, 71] or an expiry field that the decision algorithm never reads [58]. Otherwise it is a session or token lifetime rather than a consent validity window [73, 67, 51], or a claimed auto-expiry with no enforcement locus [68, 70].⦆ ⦅Verified revocation with an observed denial is reported by Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58], in a demonstration by Eneh et al. [44], and in a single narrated scenario in [68]⦆; elsewhere revocation is specified and its cost measured, but its effect on a subsequent request is not exercised [61, 62, 60]. ⦅Therefore, the gap under Req 5 is not the absence of temporal mechanisms. The gap is that the validity interval, revocation and state transitions are not enforced at the consent object itself and verified at decision time in a multi-institution exchange.⦆⦄

⦅Formal assurance of the authorisation decision is almost absent, and where it exists it is narrow. The four included studies with a formal proof, Wu and Zhang [76], Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54] and Mei et al. [55], together with the two supporting references that carry a proof, Gao et al. [48] and Luo et al. [52], prove anonymity, unforgeability, confidentiality or revocation properties of a cryptographic gate over one or two conditions. None of them contains a theorem stating that access is granted only if a conjunction of identity, authority, policy, temporal and lifecycle conditions holds, because none of them implements such a conjunction. Conversely, the studies with the broadest decision predicates, Punia et al. [61], Madine et al. [53], Ferreira et al. [45], Phuyal et al. [58], Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66] and Panagoulias et al. [57], provide at most a threat table or a structured adversary model. Across the corpus, therefore, the breadth of the decision predicate and the strength of its assurance vary inversely, and no study occupies the position in which a broad predicate is formally proved. The empirical evidence shows the same pattern from the other side. Five studies report a complete empirical evaluation [37, 47, 49, 57, 58], and only Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58] verify ALLOW and DENY outcomes systematically, the former in a single-node simulation and the latter without adversarial tests. A larger group of studies builds and measures a decision path without verifying a single authorisation decision [61, 35, 65, 72, 78, 36]. Sawant and Gomes [65] run the broadest measurement campaign in the corpus. They report no outcome for the access-control function that they formalise. When the formal and empirical halves of Req 6 are combined, nine of the 25 included studies would reach a tick in the combined Req 6 column of the tables of Section 2.4, but no study combines a formal proof of its decision with a systematic empirical test of that decision.⦆

⦅Therefore, the review establishes two gaps rather than one. The first is a conjunction gap. ⦅Identity and authority verification, collective approval, purpose and data-scope policy, temporal validity and lifecycle control each exist in the literature. Several of them exist in mature form. A number of studies combine three or four of them in one design [58, 61, 45, 66, 57].⦆ However, no study conjoins identity, authority, threshold, policy, temporal, jurisdictional and lifecycle conditions in one decision predicate in which multi-party approval is a standing condition of every access decision and in which the patient, rather than an institution, defines the approving set. The second is an assurance gap. Where the conditions do co-exist, they are neither proved nor tested as an authorisation decision, and where a proof exists it covers a fragment of the predicate. The proposed framework is positioned against these two gaps. The consent object C carries the guardian set G and the threshold N together with the identity, policy, temporal, jurisdictional and lifecycle components. The access decision is the conjunction of the corresponding predicates, and the conjunction, rather than any single component, is the object of both formal and empirical assurance. It should be noted that the framework is not positioned on the idea of an evaluable consent object, which the literature has provided since 2020 [71, 37], nor on the existence of a threshold mechanism, which the six classes above provide. It is positioned on the conjunction of the conditions and on the assurance of that conjunction.⦆

title: Research Gaps in the Existing Studies from the Requirement Perspective

text: ⦃Gap 1 (Req 1): The strongest evaluable consent objects in the reviewed studies are the purpose-based tuple of Tith et al. [71], the ontology object of Albalwy et al. [37], the on-chain consent object of Phuyal et al. [58], the consent token of Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66], the rule structure of Eneh et al. [44] and the policy object of Panagoulias et al. [57]. Each of them carries a subset of the required components: Tith et al. [71] and Albalwy et al. [37] carry no temporal component, Eneh et al. [44] and Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66] carry no authority requirement beyond the single patient, and Phuyal et al. [58] store an expiry that the decision algorithm does not read. ⦅In the 13 included studies coded as partial, and in the supporting references, the consent is⦆ a Boolean flag, a logged event or a status that is displayed rather than evaluated [36, 60, 65, 74], and in Punia et al. [61] the object that carries a lifecycle is the policy rather than the consent. What remains open is a consent object that represents the participating identities, the authority requirement including the guardian set and the threshold, the purpose and data scope, the validity interval, the jurisdiction, the lifecycle state and the evidence as separately evaluable components. This gap corresponds to research question RQ1 of Chapter 3.⦄

⦃Gap 2 (Req 2): ⦅The clearest separations of identity from authority are found in five places. In Ekholm et al. [43] and Hagström et al. [47] guardianship is verified against a national population register independently of the eID login. In Phuyal et al. [58] a licensing-body credential asserts role and scope of practice separately from the wallet identity. In Wu and Zhang [76] a zero-knowledge proof binds the owner's authorisation to a specific requester key. Separate authority evidence is also found in Tan et al. [69], Madine et al. [53] and Tseng et al. [73].⦆ ⦅In the 18 included studies coded as partial the identity is⦆ a wallet address or a platform certificate, the role is administratively assigned or self-selected at login [36, 44], and the authority to act on behalf of a patient is not evidenced at all. The register-based guardian verification of [43, 47] is centralised, and the DID and VC designs [58, 45, 66] carry no guardian credential. What remains open is decentralised evidence of both identity and authority for every participant in a consent, including the guardians, with the two conditions evaluated separately. This gap corresponds to research question RQ2 of Chapter 3.⦄

⦃Gap 3 (Req 3): The strongest multi-party mechanisms are those of Madine et al. [53], Tan et al. [69], Punia et al. [61], Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54] and Ekholm et al. [43], with partial mechanisms in Wu et al. [75], Hagström et al. [47], Al Amin et al. [38] and Abbasi et al. [35]. ⦅As set out above, the joint approval in these studies is limited in one of four ways. In some studies it is contingent on the absence of the patient [53, 69, 54], or it is reserved for particular request classes and bypassable in an emergency [61]. In others it is placed among consumer-side delegates or institution-side investigators rather than patient-side parties [50, 75], or it is applied at consent registration rather than at each access decision [43, 47, 38].⦆ None of the six mechanism classes is conjoined with a purpose or data-scope condition, and the two threshold gates that are formally proved [50, 54] are proved in isolation from any policy, temporal or lifecycle condition. What remains open is a verifiable threshold over a patient-defined approving set that is a standing component of the access-decision predicate and is evaluated on every request. This gap corresponds to research question RQ3 of Chapter 3.⦄

⦃Gap 4 (Req 4): ⦅The strongest policy enforcement is found in Eneh et al. [44], whose on-chain rules evaluate purpose, data category, sensitivity, jurisdiction and action with deny-by-default, and in Panagoulias et al. [57], who verify a purpose conjunct over thousands of requests. Román-Martínez et al. [63], Tith et al. [71], Albalwy et al. [37] and Jaiman and Urovi [49] evaluate purpose against the consent. The key-derivation scheme of [64] binds role and consent into the key, and the attribute policy of Punia et al. [61] is evaluated in a conjunctive predicate.⦆ ⦅In the remaining studies the policy is bound to the requester's role or attributes or to the ciphertext rather than to what the patient authorised [46, 56, 78, 36]. Alternatively, the purpose is captured for audit but not adjudicated [72, 73]. In other cases the policy is described but not enforced [39, 41, 59].⦆ Jurisdiction appears as a rule attribute only in Eneh et al. [44], and the declared purpose is never attested. What remains open is a purpose and data-scope policy that is bound to the consent object, evaluated together with the jurisdiction on every request, and conjoined with the multi-party approval condition. This gap corresponds to research question RQ4 of Chapter 3.⦄

⦃Gap 5 (Req 5): Temporal validity is enforced inside the decision by Eneh et al. [44], the scheme in [64], Madine et al. [53], Punia et al. [61] and Panagoulias et al. [57], credential or attribute expiry is enforced by Li et al. [51] and Mei et al. [55], and age windows are demonstrably enforced in the national portal studied by Hagström et al. [47]. Explicit lifecycle state machines are found in Phuyal et al. [58], Wu et al. [75] and Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66], and verified revocation in Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58]. ⦅However, the enforced window is usually attached to a token, a key or a credential rather than to the consent [73, 51, 77]. The stored expiry of the consent is not read by the decision [58], and revocation does not invalidate tokens already issued [73]. No study verifies expiry, revocation and state transition together at the consent level in a multi-institution exchange.⦆ What remains open is the enforcement of the validity interval, immediate and verifiable revocation, and controlled transitions between lifecycle states of the consent object itself at every access decision. This gap corresponds to research question RQ5 of Chapter 3.⦄

⦃Gap 6 (Req 6): Formal proofs are provided by Wu and Zhang [76], Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54], Mei et al. [55], Gao et al. [48] and Luo et al. [52], in each case for a cryptographic property of a narrow predicate. Complete empirical evaluations are provided by Panagoulias et al. [57], Phuyal et al. [58], Albalwy et al. [37], Jaiman and Urovi [49] and Hagström et al. [47], and systematic adversarial testing without formal content by Tremper et al. [72] and Sawant and Gomes [65]. ⦅No study provides both. The studies with the broadest predicates [61, 53, 45, 66] provide neither a proof nor an ALLOW and DENY test of the decision, and Phuyal et al. [58], which does test both outcomes, provides no formal argument.⦆⦅⦆ What remains open is the formal definition and proof of the properties of the conjoined predicate, namely identity correctness, authorisation integrity, threshold security, temporal safety and lifecycle safety, together with an empirical evaluation that demonstrates the refusal of the negative cases. This gap corresponds to research question RQ6 of Chapter 3.⦄
